guides.title: Hindu and Muslim histories in South Asia
guides.description: From Malabar’s merchant ports to Mughal courts and colonial Punjab, Hindu and Muslim lives intersected through trade, worship, law, political alliances and conflict.
guides.intro: A copper-plate grant from Malabar, a Persian translation of the Mahabharata and a weaver’s songs offer different views of religious life in South Asia. Merchant records, court documents and survivor testimony show how relations changed with the institutions and politics of each place.
guides.scope: Selected episodes from the early medieval period through the British Raj. A separate epilogue in this guide covers the 1947 Partition, after the atlas timeline ends in 1934.

map.scope: Modern terrain with approximate locations of places discussed in the guide. The Lahore marker also covers the guide’s 1947 epilogue.

points.label: Kollam, Malabar Coast
points.description: The Kollam copper plates record a grant that brings several religious communities in a trading port into view.

points.label: Qutb complex, Delhi
points.description: The congregational mosque incorporates pillars from earlier Hindu and Jain temples.

points.label: Uch Sharif, Punjab
points.description: Tombs associated with Sufi lineages include that of Bibi Jawindi, remembered for the piety and influence she carried within one such lineage.

points.label: Bagerhat, Bengal delta
points.description: The surviving mosques, tanks and tomb mark Khan Jahan’s settlement at Khalifatabad.

points.label: Varanasi
points.description: Traditions place Kabir, the weaver and devotional poet, in or near Varanasi.

points.label: Ajmer
points.description: Akbar repeatedly traveled from his court to the shrine of the Chishti saint Muinuddin.

points.label: Fatehpur Sikri, near Agra
points.description: Akbar’s planned capital included an imperial mosque and the tomb of the Chishti saint Salim.

points.label: Bijapur, Deccan
points.description: The ruler Ibrahim Adil Shah II composed devotional and courtly songs collected in the Kitab-i Nauras.

points.label: Dhar, Malwa
points.description: Family papers show Hindu landholders using the courts of Muslim judges for disputes over property and inheritance.

points.label: Dhaka
points.description: The All-India Muslim League was founded in Dhaka, capital of Eastern Bengal and Assam at the time.

points.label: Lahore, Punjab
points.description: Akbar shifted his principal residence to Lahore in 1585. Lahore and nearby Amritsar experienced violence and refugee resettlement when Partition separated them in 1947.

paragraphs.text: In the early eighth century, Umayyad armies under Muhammad ibn Qasim conquered parts of Sindh in the lower Indus valley. The Persian Chachnama was written centuries later. Historian Manan Ahmed Asif reads it in the context of thirteenth-century Sindh, where its stories of conquest were also arguments about how rulers should govern a religiously diverse society.

Muslim traders settled in Malabar’s ports, which had links to Arabia and the wider Indian Ocean. The Kollam copper plates of 849 record a grant by a local ruler to a Christian establishment. Signatures in several scripts attest to the port’s religious diversity. A twelfth-century letter preserved in the Cairo Geniza asked a Jewish trader in southwestern India to pass news about iron prices to two Hindu associates and one Muslim associate.

After the Ghurid conquest of Delhi in the late twelfth century, Qutb al-Din Aibak began a congregational mosque at Mehrauli, reusing pillars from Hindu and Jain temples. Aibak became the first sultan of Delhi in 1206. In the fifteenth-century Bengal delta, Khalifatabad, now Bagerhat, developed mosques alongside roads and reservoirs. Historian Richard Eaton links the later growth of Muslim communities in eastern Bengal to agricultural expansion. Some Mughal land grants required recipients to cultivate the land and maintain a mosque or shrine.

In the sixteenth-century Deccan, Vijayanagara’s ruler Rama Raya exploited rivalries among neighbouring sultanates, dealing with rulers and nobles across religious lines. In 1565 several of those sultanates joined against him at Talikota, defeated his army and sacked his capital.

sections.heading: Mughal rule and the politics of patronage

paragraphs.text: Akbar’s court drew some Rajput houses into the empire through marriage and military service. Other Rajput rulers faced imperial campaigns. Near Agra at Fatehpur Sikri, his court built a mosque, a Sufi tomb and palaces that drew on different architectural traditions. In 1582 he commissioned the Persian Razmnama, a translation of the Sanskrit epic Mahabharata. Surviving illustrated copies show how the imperial workshop made that epic available in a new language and visual form.

In 1670 Aurangzeb ordered the destruction of Mathura’s Keshava Deva temple. Eaton situates the attack in the context of rebellion near Mathura and reads the targeting of politically prominent temples as an expression of imperial power in religious terms. In the 1660s, two provincial governors under Aurangzeb granted resources to priests who served at the Mahakaleshwar temple in Ujjain.

At Ajmer the tomb of Muinuddin Chishti drew Muslim and Hindu pilgrims to a shrine of the Chishti Sufi order. Akbar repeatedly offered gifts and alms there between 1562 and 1579. The journeys also gave him opportunities to form alliances and assert authority. At Uch Sharif in southern Punjab, the tomb of Bibi Jawindi commemorates a woman remembered for her piety and influence within a Sufi lineage.

Bhakti, devotion to the divine, took many forms. The songs associated with Kabir, remembered as a weaver from a Muslim family in Varanasi, address a formless divine and criticize caste prejudice and sectarian pride. Communities have passed down different versions of his songs. In Bijapur, Sultan Ibrahim Adil Shah II’s Kitab-i Nauras invoked Saraswati, the Hindu goddess of music and learning, alongside Muslim holy figures.

Legal papers from a family of Hindu landholders in Dhar, central India, show them using courts presided over by Muslim judges. In one inheritance dispute a judge apportioned shares without referring to the family’s religion. The surviving papers offer a view from a property-owning family, whose access to courts is easier to trace than that of landless neighbours.

In colonial Punjab, official returns recorded members of some subordinated caste groups as Hindu, Muslim, Sikh or Christian. Religious affiliation offered ways to organize and claim a different social position. In the countryside, dependence on dominant landowners and restrictions on access to land continued to shape what working families could change.

From the late nineteenth century, British census officials sought to place people in standardized categories of caste and religion. The results gave officials and political organizers figures for the size of communities. The 1909 Morley–Minto reforms gave Muslim voters on designated rolls separate electorates for some legislative seats, giving religious identification a formal role in political representation.

In 1905 British authorities divided Bengal and made Dhaka the capital of Eastern Bengal and Assam. The All-India Muslim League was founded in Dhaka the following year. The division provoked opposition and was reversed in 1911. After the First World War, Gandhi and Congress joined Khilafat activists, who sought to preserve the Ottoman caliphate, in the Non-Cooperation campaign against British rule.

In 1921 Muslim Mappila peasants in Malabar rose against colonial authority amid long-standing conflicts over land and rent. Some rebels attacked Hindu civilians and temples. British forces suppressed the uprising, and colonial courts imposed mass convictions.

cells: Muhammad ibn Qasim’s campaigns bring parts of the lower Indus under Umayyad rule.
A land grant preserves evidence of multiple trading communities on the Malabar Coast.
Qutb al-Din Aibak begins the Quwwat al-Islam mosque after the Ghurid conquest.
Aibak establishes an independent sultanate after the death of the Ghurid ruler.
Khalifatabad develops around mosques, roads and reservoirs in the Bengal delta.
Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi, the sultan of Delhi, and lays the foundations of Mughal rule in northern India.
A coalition of Deccan sultanates defeats Vijayanagara. Its capital is subsequently sacked.
Akbar commissions a Persian translation of the Sanskrit Mahabharata.
Aurangzeb orders the demolition of the Keshava Deva temple.
The Morley–Minto reforms introduce separate Muslim electorates.
Khilafat organizers and Congress combine in the Non-Cooperation campaign.
The Mappila rebellion challenges British authority and includes attacks on Hindu civilians and places of worship.

paragraphs.text: As British rule ended in August 1947, Partition created independent India and Pakistan and divided Punjab and Bengal. The boundary awards became public after independence. Lahore and Amritsar, neighbouring cities separated by the new border, experienced attacks, forced departures and refugee resettlement. Across the new states millions fled or moved. Hindu, Muslim and Sikh families lost relatives and homes. Survivor testimony also documents abduction, forced marriage and other sexual violence.

In Punjab the upheaval around the transfer of power was especially concentrated. Bengal saw waves of displacement over a longer period, with Hindu refugees leaving East Bengal and Muslims moving east from India. Who could remain or return depended on local security, property and the policies of the new states.
